intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. The notes under each slide explain it, tell you what to remember and warn you where people slip. Work the examples in pencil before you read the steps, and answer the recall questions from memory.

sections.title: What Environmental Justice Is
sections.big_idea: Environmental justice asks **who bears the harm and who gets the benefit**, and who was in the room when the decision was made.
in_plain_words: The deck defines justice as the fair distribution of environmental benefits and burdens, and the meaningful inclusion of all communities in the decisions that shape their environment. Its slogan, where we live, work, play and pray, moved the environment from distant wilderness to everyday surroundings and brought labour and civil-rights organisers into the movement.

Two contrasts sharpen the idea. Conservation protects habitat, while the justice lens asks who depends on the forest, who is displaced and who decides. Environmentalism of the poor adds that Southern struggles are about livelihood and survival. **Procedure matters as much as location**, since a community never consulted has suffered an injustice before the first tree falls.

left.title: Conservation lens
items: Sees people as a pressure on nature

right.title: Justice lens
items: Sees people as part of the ecosystem
Remedy: recognised rights over the commons

key_terms.meaning: Fair sharing of environmental benefits and burdens, with all communities included in decisions.
Protecting nature by evicting the people who live in it, as in a tiger reserve.
Removing forest communities to create a protected area: a gain and an injustice.
Southern struggles over livelihood, water, forests and clean air.
Would this be sited here if the people deciding lived here?

worked_example.title: Technical or justice question?
worked_example.setup: A colleague lists four questions about a new plant. Sort each into a technical question or an environmental justice question.
steps: Is the river polluted? That asks about the environment.
Who lives downstream of the outfall? That is an environmental justice question.
Was the plant approved? That asks about compliance.
Who was in the room when it was approved? That is an environmental justice question.
worked_example.answer: Questions 2 and 4 are the environmental justice questions, and the course is about those.

mistakes: Treating environmental harm as a technical surprise. The slide calls it an allocation, and allocations have authors.
Equating conservation with justice. A tiger reserve can be ecologically sound and unjust at once.
Assuming a green project is automatically just. Solar parks displace pastoralists.
Counting a hearing as consultation. Recorded objections that change nothing satisfy the letter and none of the purpose.

recall.q: How does the deck define environmental justice?
recall.a: The fair distribution of environmental benefits and burdens, and the meaningful inclusion of all communities in the decisions that shape their environment.

recall.q: What did the slogan 'where we live, work, play and pray' change?
recall.a: It moved the environment from distant wilderness to everyday surroundings and brought labour and civil-rights groups into the movement.

recall.q: What is the practical siting test?
recall.a: Would this project be sited here if the people deciding lived here?

recall.q: How can you test whether a consultation was real?
recall.a: Ask what it changed.

sections.title: Origins of the Movement
sections.big_idea: The movement began with **bodies on the road and arms around trees**: local, led by the affected, and older than the term.
in_plain_words: Warren County in 1982 gave the US movement its spark, and Benjamin Chavis named the pattern environmental racism. The 1987 report found race the strongest predictor of hazardous-waste siting, even after accounting for income, which made the term defensible.

India has its own roots in Chipko, Silent Valley, Bhopal, Narmada and later struggles. Across the origin cases the harm fell on the marginalised, the decision was taken elsewhere, resistance was local and recognition came late. Silent Valley is the contrast, since few people lived there. **The affected organised first**, and the professionals arrived afterwards.

events.what: Bhopal gas leak; Silent Valley park

key_terms.meaning: Disproportionate siting of hazards in communities of colour, and their exclusion from decisions.
1982 PCB landfill protest in North Carolina, remembered as the movement's birthplace.
1973 Himalayan movement in which villagers embraced trees to stop felling.
December 1984 gas leak from Union Carbide; contamination and justice remain unfinished.
Kerala rainforest saved from a dam; declared a national park in 1984.

worked_example.title: Which case breaks the pattern?
worked_example.setup: Check three cases against the shared features: harm on the marginalised, a decision taken elsewhere, local resistance, and livelihood tied to ecology.
steps: Chipko: villagers faced contractors and defended fuel, fodder and landslide protection. All the features fit.
Bhopal: poor settlements pressed against the plant gates carried the risk. Harm on the marginalised fits.
Silent Valley: scientists, writers and citizens campaigned, and the forest was largely uninhabited.
The slide says the politics differ when people do not live where the harm lands.
worked_example.answer: Silent Valley is the exception: a conservation win without displacement, where few people lived.

mistakes: Treating environmental justice as an American import. The slide says the struggles are older than the term.
Retelling Chipko as a conservation story. It began as a dispute over who may use the forest.
Reading a failed protest as a failure. Warren County lost the landfill fight and started a movement.
Skipping the evidence step. The 1987 finding let the claim stand against a land-price explanation.

recall.q: What happened in Warren County in 1982?
recall.a: North Carolina chose a poor, majority-Black county for PCB-contaminated soil, over 500 people were arrested and the landfill went ahead.

recall.q: What did the 1987 report find?
recall.a: Race was the strongest predictor of hazardous-waste siting, even after accounting for income.

recall.q: Who coined 'environmental racism'?
recall.a: Benjamin Chavis.

recall.q: What did Silent Valley show?
recall.a: That a movement could win and defend a forest without displacement, because few people lived there.

recall.q: Name the four features shared by the origin cases.
recall.a: Harm on the poor and marginalised; decisions taken elsewhere; local, embodied resistance; livelihood and ecology inseparable.

sections.title: Three Dimensions and a Fourth
sections.big_idea: Justice has three faces: **who bears the harm, who decides, and whose claims count**. A struggle can win one and lose the others.
in_plain_words: Distributive justice asks who gets the harm and who gets the benefit. Procedural justice asks about information, consultation and the power to influence the outcome. Recognition justice asks whether a community is seen as having standing, knowledge and rights at all.

Recognition decides the other two: a community not recognised as having rights is not consulted, and a community not consulted receives the harm. A fourth lens, intergenerational justice, adds time and irreversibility. Compensation can settle distribution and leave the rest untouched, so **name the dimension your campaign is fighting on**.

diagram.root: Three faces of justice, plus time

children.label: Distributive
items: Won by relocating or preventing it

children.label: Recognition
items: Won by legal and social status

key_terms.meaning: Fair allocation of environmental goods and bads across people and places.
Fair, inclusive, transparent decisions, with real power to influence the outcome.
Respect for the identity, knowledge, culture and rights of affected communities.
Fairness across time, including what is foreclosed for people not yet here.
Valuing future costs lower; a high rate makes distant harm look almost costless.

worked_example.title: Audit a relocation package
worked_example.setup: Hypothetical: a village is relocated with a generous cash package, but nobody asked its Gram Sabha and its sacred land was treated as empty.
steps: Distribution: cash was paid, so the measurable loss was priced.
Procedure: there was no consultation, so the process failed.
Recognition: the sacred land was treated as empty, so the community's claim went unrecognised.
Intergenerational: ask what is foreclosed for the next generation, such as grazing and water.
worked_example.answer: A distributive win with procedural and recognition defeats, which communities often experience as no win at all.

mistakes: Treating a compensation package as justice. It answers the distributive question only.
Fixing a recognition problem with a better offer. The slide says a better package does not solve it.
Calling a hearing procedural justice when it is held late, far away and in the wrong language.
Presenting a high discount rate as neutral arithmetic. It is a value choice.

recall.q: What are the three dimensions and their questions?
recall.a: Distributive: who bears the harm. Procedural: who decides. Recognition: whose claims count.

recall.q: Which dimension decides the other two?
recall.a: Recognition.

recall.q: Why is irreversibility the stronger intergenerational argument?
recall.a: A drawn-down aquifer or a lost species is a foreclosed option that compensation cannot restore.

recall.q: What does the table say compensation cannot address?
recall.a: A sacred site, a livelihood on the commons, a dispersed social network, and never having been asked.

sections.title: Who Bears the Burden
sections.big_idea: In India, harm follows **caste, tribe, class and gender**, and the burdens stack on the same people.
in_plain_words: Where the US movement names race, the Indian reality is structured by caste, tribe and class. Dalit and Adivasi communities are disproportionately exposed to polluted land, hazardous work and displacement. Sacrifice zones form where land is cheap, residents lack political weight and one polluter makes the next easier.

Manual scavenging and waste picking show harm assigned by social identity. Women absorb scarcity as unpaid labour, and mineral wealth lies under Adivasi homelands. The burdens compound, as with a poor Adivasi woman in a mining district, so **look at the axes together** and test any intervention against the most burdened.

key_terms.meaning: Scholars' term for harm that falls along caste lines.
A place and its people treated as expendable for industry or growth.
Banned manual cleaning of excreta, still done almost entirely by Dalits.
The combined effect of successive projects, which each clearance rarely assesses.
Records of unpaid time, such as walking for water, that assessments omit.

worked_example.title: Which axis explains the burden?
worked_example.setup: Sort four situations by the axis the slides use to explain them.
steps: A tannery on a riverbank, worked by those at the bottom of the caste order: caste.
Walking further for water when a well dries: gender, since unpaid provisioning falls on women.
Bauxite under forest homelands: indigeneity and the geography of Scheduled Areas.
Compensation registered in a husband's name: gender again, on top of the displacement an Adivasi family faces.
worked_example.answer: Caste, gender, indigeneity, and gender compounding indigeneity. Several axes can act on one person.

mistakes: Importing the US frame unchanged. Redlining and zoning translate into settlement patterns by caste and 'wasteland' classification.
Reporting outcomes by caste and separately by gender. That misses the woman who belongs to both groups.
Treating manual scavenging as an occupational-safety issue. The root is caste, so mechanisation alone has not ended it.
Quoting the illustrative charts as statistics. The slides label them illustrative.

recall.q: What do some scholars call the Indian pattern of harm along caste lines?
recall.a: Environmental casteism.

recall.q: Name three sacrifice zones or clusters from the deck.
recall.a: Singrauli's coal-ash belt, Vapi and Ankleshwar, and tanneries along riverbanks.

recall.q: Why does formalising waste handling often hurt waste pickers?
recall.a: Municipal contracts transfer the work to a company and remove the livelihood of those already doing it.

recall.q: Why must you look at several axes together?
recall.a: Caste, class, gender and indigeneity compound, so one-axis disaggregation misses people who sit on several.

sections.title: Climate Justice
sections.big_idea: Those who caused least suffer most, and **the measure you lead with decides who is asked to cut**.
in_plain_words: Climate justice extends the frame to the planet. CBDR says all states must act, but those who emitted more and can do more must do more. India's emissions look large in total and small per person and cumulatively, so choosing which measure to lead with is a justice choice.

Loss and damage names harm that adaptation cannot prevent and asks who pays. A finite carbon budget raises distribution again: equal per-capita shares, grandfathering, historical adjustment or capability. **Every allocation rule is a moral position.** Adaptation capacity is also unequal, and the poor have the least of it.

left.title: By total
items: India is among the largest emitters
1.4 billion people make the total large
Supports pressure on India to act

key_terms.meaning: Common but differentiated responsibilities: all states act, those with more history and capacity do more.
The finite remaining emissions that keep warming within safe limits.
Allocating the budget by current emissions; the default, and it favours today's biggest emitters.
Harm from climate change that adaptation cannot prevent, with a claim for help bearing it.
Buffers, protection, choice, mobility and voice that let people cope.

worked_example.title: Total against per person
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: Country A has 100 million people emitting 1,000 million tonnes a year. Country B has 1,000 million people emitting 3,000 million tonnes.
steps: By total, B emits 3,000 million tonnes against A's 1,000 million, so B looks like the bigger emitter.
Per person in A: 1,000 ÷ 100 = 10 tonnes.
Per person in B: 3,000 ÷ 1,000 = 3 tonnes.
Both statements are true. Which one you lead with decides who is asked to cut.
worked_example.answer: B has the larger total and A the larger per-person footprint, so the lead measure is a justice choice.

mistakes: Arguing from one measure as if the others were false. The slide says all four are true at once.
Calling loss and damage adaptation. It names harm adaptation cannot prevent.
Treating grandfathering as neutral. It favours whoever emits most now.
Quoting the emissions charts as exact. The slides call the figures approximate or illustrative.

recall.q: What does CBDR stand for and where does it come from?
recall.a: Common but differentiated responsibilities, a principle of the UNFCCC (1992).

recall.q: Why are emissions a stock?
recall.a: Warming reflects cumulative historical emissions attributable to specific economies over specific periods.

recall.q: What distinguishes loss and damage from adaptation?
recall.a: Loss and damage is harm adaptation cannot prevent, and it implies liability.

recall.q: Which carbon-budget rule locks in existing inequality?
recall.a: Grandfathering current emissions.

recall.q: Why do the poor have less adaptation capacity?
recall.a: They lack financial buffers, physical protection, occupational choice, mobility and political voice.

sections.title: Land, Forest & the Commons
sections.big_idea: The commons are the poorest households' safety net, and **the law now recognises what colonial settlement failed to record**.
in_plain_words: Fuel, fodder, grazing, water and forest produce come from commons that nobody holds title to, so their loss counts as zero in compensation. Colonial forest law recast long-time users as encroachers, and the Forest Rights Act names that historical injustice as the wrong it repairs.

The FRA puts the Gram Sabha in charge of initiating and verifying claims, and PESA gives Scheduled Area Gram Sabhas a voice before acquisition and mining. Displacement continues, with tens of millions affected since 1947 and no full count. The LARR Act promised more than it delivered. **Ask what happened to the last project's displaced.**

diagram.caption: from the colonial wrong to the recognition Act

key_terms.meaning: Village forests, grazing land, ponds, rivers and fisheries used collectively.
FRA rights to manage a forest; far fewer recognised than eligible.
The full village assembly that initiates and verifies FRA claims.
1996 Act extending self-rule to Scheduled Areas; state rules vary.
The legal phrase that lets the state compel an acquisition.

worked_example.title: Which law gives the Gram Sabha standing?
worked_example.setup: Three villages face a project. Decide which Act gives the Gram Sabha standing in each.
steps: A forest village outside any Scheduled Area faces a diversion: the FRA gives standing over forest land, including outside Scheduled Areas.
A village in a Scheduled Area faces land acquisition for a mine: PESA gives consultation before acquisition and mining.
A forest village inside a Scheduled Area: both Acts apply, so read them together.
worked_example.answer: FRA, PESA, and both together. State rules decide how far PESA actually reaches.

mistakes: Valuing common land at zero because nobody holds title. Compensation attaches to title, so the loss goes unrecorded.
Reading the FRA as granting new rights. It recognises rights colonial settlement failed to record.
Treating PESA as uniform across states. State rules vary and several dilute the Act.
Counting cash as rehabilitation. LARR's higher compensation is the best-implemented provision and rehabilitation the least.

recall.q: Why does the FRA call itself a recognition Act?
recall.a: It recognises rights the colonial settlement failed to record, which is a different legal claim from granting new ones.

recall.q: Which part of the FRA is under-implemented?
recall.a: Community forest rights.

recall.q: What powers does PESA give the Gram Sabha?
recall.a: Safeguarding community resources and customs, consultation before acquisition and mining, and control of minor minerals and forest produce.

recall.q: What share of India's population are Adivasis?
recall.a: About 8.6% (Census 2011).

recall.q: What are the five questions of the just test?
recall.a: Public purpose, consent, alternatives, rehabilitation, and what happened afterwards to the people from the last project.

sections.title: Pollution & Health
sections.big_idea: Pollution lands on the poor, its health cost is **under-attributed**, and poverty and exposure feed each other.
in_plain_words: Air, water and soil pollution are among India's largest causes of premature death. India's national PM2.5 standard of 40 µg/m³ is eight times the WHO guideline of 5. Within a city the poor live nearer traffic and industry, cook with biomass and work outdoors, so a city average describes nobody.

Fluoride and arsenic are geogenic, yet the injustice is who has a safe alternative source. E-waste is burned and acid-bathed by informal workers, and industrial clusters tie households to the plants that pollute them. Poverty, exposure and lost earnings form a cycle, and **recognised land rights, enforceable objection and community data** break it.

key_terms.meaning: Fine particulate matter in µg/m³; the WHO annual guideline is 5.
Coming from the rock, as fluoride and arsenic do; the harm has no polluter.
Wood and dung burned for cooking; indoor smoke harms women and children.
Extended Producer Responsibility rules meant to divert e-waste to formal recycling.
Share of illness and death attributable to environmental hazards.

worked_example.title: Standard against guideline
worked_example.setup: The deck gives a WHO guideline of 5 µg/m³ and a national standard of 40 µg/m³. The city reading in the last two steps is illustrative.
steps: Standard against guideline: 40 ÷ 5 = 8.
A city at 80 µg/m³ against the national standard: 80 ÷ 40 = 2.
The same city against the WHO guideline: 80 ÷ 5 = 16.
worked_example.answer: Meeting the national standard still means eight times the guideline. A city at 80 µg/m³ is twice the standard and 16 times the guideline.

mistakes: Reporting against the national standard alone. Compliance with Indian law is different from safety.
Using a city average. It describes nobody and hides the five differences between residents.
Assuming rural air is clean. Exposure in the Indo-Gangetic plain is comparable, but monitoring stations are urban.
Cleaning one plant and calling the cycle broken. Without changes to siting, tenure and voice, the pattern moves.

recall.q: What are the WHO and Indian PM2.5 standards?
recall.a: WHO: 5 µg/m³. India: 40 µg/m³, eight times higher.

recall.q: Why are fluoride and arsenic still injustices when they are geogenic?
recall.a: The harm has no author, but who gets a safe alternative source is a social question.

recall.q: What did tube wells do in the Bengal delta?
recall.a: They were promoted to avoid surface-water pathogens and drew from arsenic-bearing aquifers.

recall.q: Why are industrial-cluster communities hard to organise?
recall.a: The polluter is also the employer, and households depend on the wage.

recall.q: Name two intervention points that break the pollution cycle.
recall.a: Any two of: recognised land rights, enforceable objection at siting, data communities can produce themselves.

sections.title: Just Transition
sections.big_idea: A just transition **decarbonises without abandoning workers**, and sequencing decides whether it works.
in_plain_words: Coal anchors states like Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and West Bengal through direct jobs, a far larger contract workforce, local services, royalties and railway freight. Plans count the formal miners and miss the informal majority. Retraining announced at closure is too late, and reclamation liability should be secured before mining begins.

Green jobs are not automatically fair: they may be elsewhere, need other skills, be fewer or be worse. Renewables need land, often labelled wasteland, so **the consent standards demanded of mines and dams apply to solar parks too**. Energy justice also means access for the many who still have too little, and clean cooking fuel brings the largest immediate health gain.

diagram.caption: the plan must cover the whole belt

key_terms.meaning: Leaving fossil fuels while protecting workers and communities that depend on them.
The far larger informal coal workforce that transition plans miss.
Responsibility for restoring mined land; secure it before mining begins.
Administrative label for land with no recognised owner; it erases commons users.
Access, reliability, affordability and clean cooking fuel for those with too little.

worked_example.title: Who does the plan count?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a coalfield has 10,000 formal miners and 30,000 contract workers. The deck says contract labour is far larger.
steps: All livelihoods in mining: 10,000 + 30,000 = 40,000.
A plan that counts only formal miners covers 10,000 ÷ 40,000 = 0.25 of them.
The share left uncounted: 1 − 0.25 = 0.75.
worked_example.answer: A plan counting only formal staff covers 25% of the workforce and misses 75%.

mistakes: Counting only formal employees. Contract labour is far larger and appears in no employment record.
Comparing national job totals between coal and renewables. Equal numbers can mean total loss in one district.
Treating 'wasteland' as empty land. The slide says there is no such thing.
Announcing retraining at closure. The same programme two years earlier is a transition.

recall.q: What five questions does a just transition ask?
recall.a: Who loses work; what replaces it and where; who pays for retraining; what happens to the land; who decides.

recall.q: Why do coal states resist transition?
recall.a: They lose royalty income as well as jobs.

recall.q: What four reasons make green jobs not automatically just?
recall.a: They may be elsewhere, need different skills, be fewer, or be worse.

recall.q: Which clean-energy item has the largest immediate health return?
recall.a: Clean cooking fuel.

recall.q: Where should reclamation liability sit?
recall.a: Secured before mining begins, through a bond or escrow.

sections.title: Movements & Resistance
sections.big_idea: Almost every Indian environmental protection was **won by a movement**, and that shows where a practitioner should expect change to come from.
in_plain_words: Chipko, Silent Valley, Niyamgiri and the Narmada struggle each won something: a felling ban, a park, Gram Sabha consent, scrutiny of resettlement. The Narmada movement lost the dam and changed the rules. Niyamgiri shows recognition justice working through law, and anti-POSCO shows the FRA as a shield.

Fisherfolk, anti-nuclear, anti-mining, urban and river movements share a structure: local, led by those affected and contesting a decision taken elsewhere. PIL opens the courts, with limits on enforcement. Defending the environment can be dangerous, and **the risk falls on local activists**, so weigh it with the community.

key_terms.meaning: Movement against large Narmada dams over displacement without rehabilitation.
2013 ruling sending the mining decision to the Gram Sabhas.
Adivasi community for whom the Niyamgiri hills are sacred.
Petition letting any public-spirited person approach the courts for those who cannot.
Activist who faces intimidation, criminalisation or violence for protecting the commons.

worked_example.title: Match each movement to its win
worked_example.setup: Match four movements to what they achieved, using the slides.
steps: Chipko: a felling ban in the region.
Silent Valley: the dam was dropped and a national park declared in 1984.
Niyamgiri: the Supreme Court referred the decision to the Gram Sabhas, and every one rejected it.
Narmada: the dam was built, yet the World Bank withdrew and lender rules on resettlement changed.
worked_example.answer: Four kinds of win, one of them from a movement that lost its object but changed the rules.

mistakes: Treating protections as permanent. They can be reversed through amendment, exemption and non-enforcement.
Calling Narmada a failure. It lost the dam and changed the rules.
Filing a PIL first. It forecloses the cheaper options.
Planning tactics for a community without weighing the risk with them.

recall.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in the Niyamgiri case?
recall.a: In 2013 it ruled the Gram Sabhas should decide on the bauxite mine, and every village voted no.

recall.q: What did the World Bank do over Narmada?
recall.a: It withdrew after an independent review.

recall.q: What did anti-POSCO rely on?
recall.a: The Forest Rights Act and the Gram Sabha.

recall.q: What are the limits of PIL?
recall.a: Enforcement is uneven, it is slow and costly to sustain, and it can antagonise a government you may need.

recall.q: Why are fishing communities among the least visible affected groups?
recall.a: The resource is common, mobile and unmeasured, and there is no title to a fishery.

sections.title: Principles & Legal Tools
sections.big_idea: Law is a tool: **polluter pays, precaution, public trust and Article 21** give the principles, and RTI, EIA, the NGT and PIL give the routes.
in_plain_words: Polluter pays puts the cost of prevention and remedy on the cause, and fails when fines are cheaper than compliance. Precaution shifts the burden of proof to the proponent where harm may be serious or irreversible. Public trust makes the state a trustee of rivers, forests and seashores, and Article 21 anchors a right to a healthy environment.

The NGT combines judicial and expert members, but access is hard from remote districts. The EIA is procedural justice on paper, with consultants paid by the proponent. Rights of nature remains emergent. Sequence the tools: **documents first, objection on record second, tribunal third, constitutional litigation last**.

diagram.caption: each step builds the record for the next

key_terms.meaning: Polluters bear the cost of preventing, controlling and remedying pollution.
Lack of certainty is no reason to delay protection against serious or irreversible harm.
The state holds air, rivers, forests and seashores in trust for the public.
Study of a project's likely effects before clearance, with a public hearing.
Emerging idea that rivers and forests have legal standing.

worked_example.title: Order the tools for a quarry clearance
worked_example.setup: Hypothetical: a village learns that a quarry has been cleared near its forest and wants to respond.
steps: Start with RTI to obtain the clearance file, the alternatives considered and the hearing minutes.
If a hearing is still ahead, attend and put objections on record.
If the clearance is defective on procedure or merit, challenge it before the NGT.
Keep Article 21 PIL for when other routes are closed.
worked_example.answer: RTI, hearing, NGT, then PIL, so each step builds the record the next needs.

mistakes: Treating a penalty as polluter pays when the fine is cheaper than compliance. It becomes a licence fee.
Reading precaution as a veto. The qualifiers 'serious' and 'irreversible' stop that.
Arguing from Article 48A or 51A(g) alone. Only Article 21 can be litigated directly.
Skipping an EIA hearing because it is a formality. Objections on record are what later litigation builds on.

recall.q: Which judgment brought public trust into Indian law?
recall.a: The Kamal Nath judgment (1996).

recall.q: What does the precautionary principle shift?
recall.a: The burden of proof, onto the proponent to show the activity is safe.

recall.q: When was the NGT established?
recall.a: 2010, by statute.

recall.q: What is the structural problem with the EIA?
recall.a: The proponent pays for the assessment.

recall.q: What happened to the Uttarakhand ruling on the Ganga and Yamuna?
recall.a: The High Court declared them legal persons and the ruling was later stayed.

sections.title: EJ in Practice & Reading
sections.big_idea: Practice means **making the pattern visible**, centring the most burdened and giving data back to the people it came from.
in_plain_words: Community monitoring turns 'we feel sick' into evidence, and mapping sites against caste, income and health data shows the gradient an average hides. Disaggregation is the whole method. Pair low-cost sensors with a protocol and be honest about their limits.

The practitioner stance asks who bears the harm of your own project, treats consent as a process and respects local knowledge as evidence. Watch for wasteland labels, token hearings and cash that erases a way of life. The sources are CPCB data, FRA data, NGT judgments and RTI documents, and **read the Acts themselves**.

diagram.caption: data returns to those it was taken from

key_terms.meaning: Residents documenting pollution with low-cost monitors and simple protocols.
Splitting figures by caste, tribe, gender and distance so gradients show.
Free, prior and informed consent: a sequence, before the decision, with full information, and a real option to refuse.
A global map of environmental justice conflicts.
Claims filed against titles granted, by state and type.

worked_example.title: Run the five-step stance on your project
worked_example.setup: Apply the practitioner stance to a project you work on. The steps use the slide's five rules.
steps: Ask who bears the harm of your own project, by name and group.
Centre the most burdened, and ask who is hit hardest.
Treat consent as a process: before the decision, fully informed, with a real option to refuse.
Disaggregate every figure by caste, tribe, gender and distance.
Return the findings to those affected in a form they can use.
worked_example.answer: A project reviewed this way shows its burdens by group, with consent and data both traced to the affected.

mistakes: Reporting a district average. It describes nobody and is the number that gets reported.
Trusting low-cost sensors without a protocol. Their accuracy will be challenged.
Accepting a signature as consent. Consent is a sequence.
Applying the checklist to a mine and exempting your own green project.

recall.q: What is the whole method of mapping injustice?
recall.a: Disaggregation: what you do not disaggregate, you cannot see.

recall.q: How should you protect community monitoring against accuracy challenges?
recall.a: Pair sensors with a protocol, co-locate against a reference monitor where possible, and be honest about limits.

recall.q: Which data does the deck call the most under-used?
recall.a: FRA data on claims filed against titles granted, by state and type.

recall.q: What does the deck advise about FRA and PESA?
recall.a: Read the Acts themselves, because practitioners routinely misstate what they require on Gram Sabha consent.

recall.q: What are the five takeaways?
recall.a: Harm tracks caste, class and power; justice has three faces; those who caused least suffer most; law is a tool; there is no empty land.

notes.2: The agenda gives eleven sections with slide ranges, so you can **plan your reading** around the question you most need answered. Sections 1 to 3 build the framework, sections 4 to 8 apply it to burden, climate, land, pollution and transition, and sections 9 to 11 cover resistance, law and practice.
notes.4: Environmental justice asks who bears the harm and who enjoys the benefit, so treat it as **a question about allocation**. Use the paired table as a test: the first question in each pair is technical, the second is about people and power. Naming who is harmed also names who gains, which is why the field is contested.
notes.5: The slogan 'where we live, work, play and pray' moved the environment from distant wilderness to everyday surroundings. Use the table to see **what it rejected**: wilderness elsewhere, occupational exposure as a separate issue, amenity as a luxury. It also brought labour and civil-rights organisers into a movement dominated by conservation groups.
notes.6: Compare the two lenses by asking one thing: **who depends on this forest, and who decides?** Conservation protects habitat, while the justice lens protects people and their access. The tiger reserve example shows a decision can be ecologically sound and unjust at once. The lenses come apart when someone lives in the forest.
notes.7: Guha and Martinez-Alier's point is that Southern environmental struggles are about survival, so read the table as **livelihood against amenity**. A movement fighting a mine is defending income and water. Framing it as conservation misreads what its participants actually want.
notes.8: Follow the four-step flow: the benefit goes to cities and industry, the harm lands in a poor, rural, often Adivasi or Dalit area. Memorise the practical test at the end: **would this project be sited here if the people deciding lived here?** Use it on any siting decision.
notes.9: Justice covers voice as well as location. Use the three questions to audit a process: informed in time and language, able to object, consent treated as binding. The last row of the table is the common failure, so **test a consultation by asking what it changed**.
notes.10: Practitioners need this lens because programmes land on someone. The blind-spot table is a checklist of four wrong assumptions, and the slide says the second, that 'green' is automatically just, keeps recurring. **Name who bears your own project's harm** before you judge anyone else's.
notes.12: Warren County, 1982, is the origin story: a poor, majority-Black county chosen for PCB-contaminated soil, with over 500 arrests. The landfill went ahead and a movement began. The lesson is that **a local defeat can set the frame that wins later**, and the demand for evidence led to the studies that follow.
notes.13: Chavis coined 'environmental racism' after Warren County. Learn the table as claim and challenge: the pattern is racial, and the challenge asks which came first, the facility or the community. **Naming the wrong was itself an intervention**, because siting then had to be defended as having nothing to do with race.
notes.14: The 1987 report found race was the strongest predictor of hazardous-waste siting, even after accounting for income. That is **what made the term defensible**, since land price could not explain it away. The debate about which came first continues in places and does not overturn the distributional fact.
notes.15: South Asian struggles are older than the vocabulary. Use the timeline as a memory aid: Bishnoi in the 1730s, Chipko in 1973, Silent Valley, Bhopal and Narmada in the 1980s, then Niyamgiri and POSCO. **Borrowing the framework is different from borrowing the history**: the term came from the US, the tradition did not.
notes.16: Chipko is remembered as a conservation movement, but the slide says it began as a dispute over who may use the forest, with villagers wanting the timber for local use. Remember the lesson: **access struggles get retold as struggles for nature**, the substitution environmentalism of the poor argues against.
notes.17: Bhopal is the reference case for industrial risk: poor settlements pressed against the plant gates. The table shows a disaster with no finished ending, as contamination persists and compensation is contested. Keep it in mind for Section 10, where **polluter pays and precaution are argued through Bhopal**.
notes.18: Silent Valley is the contrast case: scientists, poets and citizens stopped a dam, and a national park was declared in 1984. It was winnable on ecological grounds because the forest was largely uninhabited. Notice **how different the politics are when no one lives where the harm lands**.
notes.19: Four features recur across the origin cases: harm on the marginalised, decisions taken elsewhere, local and embodied resistance, and livelihood tied to ecology. That is **what makes EJ a framework and more than a set of episodes**. Hold onto the point that affected people organised first and professionals arrived later.
notes.21: Three faces, three questions: who bears the harm, who decides, whose claims count. Use the table to match each dimension to what wins it. The warning is that a struggle can win one and lose another, so **name the dimension your campaign is fighting on** before you pick tactics.
notes.22: Distributive justice is about who gets the goods and the bads. Treat the table as a data request: a settlement map against the site, disaggregation by social line, the beneficiaries, and the alternatives considered. The last row turns a distribution into a decision, so **obtain the alternatives analysis under RTI**.
notes.23: Procedural justice needs information in time and language, real consultation, effective objection, a route to challenge and consent where law requires it. The right column shows how each fails in practice. The slide says projects are usually stopped on procedure, so **documenting a defective consultation** is more likely to succeed than arguing the merits.
notes.24: Recognition justice decides the other two. A community not recognised as having rights is not consulted, and one not consulted receives the harm, in that order. Read the table for **loaded words** such as 'wasteland' and 'encroachment', which turn use into absence.
notes.25: Read the four-step chain from non-recognition to exclusion, dumping and invisibility. The slide says the chain runs from recognition to distribution, which is why land-rights recognition changes environmental outcomes. It is self-reinforcing: **uncounted harm produces no evidence, and no evidence justifies the next siting**.
notes.26: Intergenerational justice adds time. The argument that bites is irreversibility: a drawn-down aquifer or a lost species is a foreclosed option that compensation cannot restore. Discounting is where it meets economics, because a high discount rate makes harm forty years out **almost costless on paper**.
notes.27: Use the four dimensions as a checklist on any project, including your own: distribution, procedure, recognition and the future. A project can pass one and fail the others, which is why they are listed separately. **Generous compensation with no consultation** answers a procedural wrong with a distributive fix.
notes.28: A cheque addresses distribution and leaves procedure and recognition untouched. Read the table as what money can price and what it cannot: a sacred site, a livelihood on the commons, a social network, and never having been asked. Communities can **reject adequate compensation for good reasons**.
notes.30: In India harm follows caste, tribe and class where the US movement names race. Use the table to translate the US frame: redlining becomes settlement patterns by caste, and zoning becomes land classification. The structural claim survives: **harm concentrates where social power is least**, so disaggregate accordingly.
notes.31: The chart is illustrative and the slide says so. Read it for direction: marginalised groups live closer to hazards, which research across India documents consistently. Leave the numbers unquoted. The habit to take away is to **ask which social group lives nearest** any hazard you study.
notes.32: A sacrifice zone is a place treated as expendable. Read the right-hand table as a mechanism: cheap land, weak political weight, then accumulation as the first plant eases the second. Cumulative impact assessment matters because **each clearance measures one project against a baseline that already includes the last**.
notes.33: Manual scavenging is banned by the 2013 Act and still persists, done almost entirely by Dalit communities. The slide treats it as the clearest example of **harm allocated by social identity**. Its last row is the point: the root is caste, so mechanisation alone has not ended it.
notes.34: Waste pickers do the recycling that keeps cities from drowning in waste, without protection or recognition as workers. The policy trap is in the last row: **formalisation often displaces them**. Integration is possible by registering pickers and contracting them into the system, as the slide describes.
notes.35: When the well dries or the forest recedes, women absorb the cost through walking, smoke and eating last. The slide argues the cost is hidden because the time is unpaid. Use it as the case for **time-use data in environmental assessment**, since an extra hour of water collection otherwise registers as no cost.
notes.36: Coal, bauxite and iron ore lie under the forests where Adivasi communities live. Follow the table's chain: forest law governs access, Scheduled Areas bring PESA and FRA, and poverty makes job promises weigh heavily. **The overlap of mineral wealth and settlement** explains why most resistance movements sit in one belt.
notes.37: This chart is also illustrative. Take the direction from it: marginalised groups are over-represented in settlements beside polluting sites while their share of the benefit stays small. **If you need figures, collect them for your own district** and disaggregate them.
notes.38: Burdens stack. The woman in the example faces displacement as an Adivasi, compensation in her husband's name as a woman, and no standing at the hearing, which is **not additive**. Disaggregating by one axis at a time misses her. Test an intervention by whether it works for the most burdened.
notes.40: Climate justice extends the frame to the planet: those who contributed least face the harshest floods, heat and cyclones. Use the table to match each group to its exposure. The slide adds the key idea that **emissions are a stock**, so today's warming reflects cumulative history, while future emitters decide the rest.
notes.41: CBDR is the legal expression of climate fairness: all states must act, but those who emitted more and can do more must do more. Split the phrase into its words using the table. It is **the most contested phrase in climate negotiation**, and the dispute is over how much differentiation, for how long.
notes.42: The chart compares per-capita CO₂ emissions. The slide's claim is that India sits below half the world average and far below the US, and that **per-capita framing tells a different story from totals**. The figures are approximate, so quote the pattern and cite the source when you need exact values.
notes.43: Total and per-capita statements are both true. Lead with total and India looks like a major emitter; lead with per person and the footprint looks small. The slide says the choice is **a justice choice** about who is asked to cut. Cumulative emissions carry the most moral weight and the least negotiating force.
notes.44: The chart is an illustrative split of cumulative emissions. Take the point behind it: carbon dioxide lingers for centuries, so history matters, and the industrialised North holds the largest share while India's is small relative to its population. **Use cumulative figures when responsibility is the question.**
notes.45: Loss and damage names harm that adaptation cannot prevent and asks who should help bear the cost. The distinction from adaptation is **the whole argument**, because it implies liability. The fund was agreed at COP27, and the slide says its capitalisation remains far below estimated need.
notes.46: The carbon budget is finite, so splitting it is a distributive question with no technical answer. Read the table as four rules, each favouring different countries. Grandfathering is the default because it needs no agreement, and it **favours whoever emits most now**.
notes.47: Adaptation capacity tracks wealth and voice: savings, housing, occupational choice, mobility and political voice. The last row decides the first four. Heat is the clearest South Asian case, where **outdoor workers carry the exposure** and are least represented in deciding the heat action plan.
notes.49: The commons are shared wealth that the poorest depend on most: fuel, fodder, grazing, water and forest produce. Their loss goes unrecorded because compensation attaches to title and **nobody holds title to grazing land**. Use the table to list what a village would lose if its commons were enclosed.
notes.50: Colonial forest law declared forests state property and turned long-time users into trespassers. Read the table as the law's effects: access became a permission and customary rights went unrecorded. This is why the Forest Rights Act **recognises and does not grant**, a different legal claim that needs evidence of long use.
notes.51: The FRA recognises individual and community rights. The table shows the split: individual titles are widely recognised and community forest rights far fewer. Community rights **transfer real authority** to the Gram Sabha, which is why they are the part resisted and the part to check first.
notes.52: The FRA makes the Gram Sabha the authority that initiates and verifies claims, which shifts power from the forest department. That is recognition justice written into statute. The slide warns where it fails: resolutions passed without quorum, meetings without objectors and **minutes that participants dispute**.
notes.53: PESA gives Gram Sabhas in Scheduled Areas a voice before land acquisition and mining. Its force depends on state rules, and several dilute it. Read PESA and FRA together: **PESA gives standing across Scheduled Areas and FRA gives it over forest land**, including outside them.
notes.54: Development-induced displacement covers dams, mines, industry and conservation. The slide counts tens of millions since 1947, with Adivasis over-represented, and says conservation displacement is usually left off lists. Note the data gap: **no single agency has counted comprehensively**, so estimates carry wide uncertainty.
notes.55: The slide pairs the chart with a fact: Adivasis are about 8.6% of the population (Census 2011) yet a far larger share of the displaced. The displaced share in the chart is illustrative. The finding to hold is the **absence of a reliable national count**, since no agency must keep one.
notes.56: The LARR Act promised consent, social-impact assessment and rehabilitation. The table shows the gap: consent thresholds narrowed, assessments waived, and rehabilitation least implemented. **Compensation is delivered and rehabilitation is not.** Ask what happened to the people displaced by the last project in your district.
notes.57: These five questions test any acquisition: whose public purpose, whether consent was free, prior and informed, whether alternatives were assessed, whether rehabilitation was delivered, and where the earlier displaced now live. The last question takes a day and **predicts the next group's fate** better than a promise on paper.
notes.59: Pollution is among India's largest environmental causes of premature death, and the table maps which kind falls on whom. The slide adds that the health cost is under-attributed: a death in a polluted district is recorded as cardiovascular disease, so **the burden shows only in modelled estimates**.
notes.60: The WHO annual PM2.5 guideline is 5 µg/m³ and India's national standard is 40, so meeting the standard still exceeds the guideline eightfold. Work out 40 ÷ 5 yourself. **Compliance with Indian law is different from safety.** Rural exposure in the Indo-Gangetic plain gets little attention.
notes.61: Two people in one city breathe different air, depending on distance from traffic, cooking fuel, time outdoors, ability to filter or leave, and baseline health. A city average describes nobody. This is the case for **neighbourhood-scale monitoring**, which community monitoring in Section 11 provides.
notes.62: Fluoride and arsenic come from the rock, so the harm has no author. The injustice lies in **who has a safe alternative source** and who must drink what the handpump gives. The Bengal delta case shows a public-health intervention making things worse, when tube wells reached arsenic-bearing aquifers.
notes.63: Most of India's e-waste is processed informally, by burning, acid baths and hand dismantling, exposing workers to lead, mercury and dioxins. Formal recycling cannot compete on price with people who pay in their own health. Extended Producer Responsibility helps only if collection **actually reaches the formal chain**.
notes.64: Industrial-cluster communities live with contaminated groundwater and respiratory and skin disease. The last row of the table explains why they are hard to organise: **the polluter is also the employer**. Sterlite in Thoothukudi shows where years of complaints can end. The slide links this to just transition.
notes.65: Follow the four-stage cycle: poverty pushes people to hazardous land, polluters site there, exposure causes disease and lost earnings, and poverty deepens. Single-point fixes move the pattern. The slide names the intervention points that break it: **recognised land rights, enforceable objection and community-produced data**.
notes.67: Just transition means leaving no one behind as the economy leaves fossil fuels. Use the table as five questions: who loses work, what replaces it and where, who pays for retraining, what happens to the land and who decides. The justice case and the **effectiveness case point the same way**.
notes.68: Coal supports direct jobs, a far larger contract workforce, local services, state royalties and railway freight. The group transition plans miss is **contract labour**, which appears in no employment record. Royalty loss explains why states resist transition, and unions are only part of that resistance.
notes.69: Compare the two columns as a sequence test. Done well means retraining before closure, land reclaimed and returned, local say and informal workers counted. Done badly is the reverse. **Sequencing decides which column you get**, and reclamation liability should be secured before mining begins.
notes.70: Renewable jobs are not automatically fair jobs. The table gives four reasons: they may be elsewhere, need different skills, be fewer or be worse. Equal national numbers can mean total loss in one district. Ask **where, for whom, on what terms and for how long**.
notes.71: Renewables need land, and land has people. Large solar and wind parks often sit on land labelled 'wasteland', which erases pastoralists and commons users. The slide calls this the sharpest current test of whether EJ is a framework or a slogan, so **scrutinise solar siting as you would a mine**.
notes.72: Energy justice includes access for people who have too little, reliable and affordable supply, and clean cooking fuel. Rooftop solar and mini-grids can deliver lower emissions and access together. Clean cooking fuel carries the **largest immediate health return** on the slide.
notes.73: Use the five principles as a test for any transition plan: workers at the table early, funded retraining, a diversified local economy, restored land and informal workers counted. The slide says to check the **informal workers row first**, because formal coal employment is a fraction of the livelihoods a coalfield supports.
notes.75: Behind almost every Indian environmental protection stands a movement, so understanding EJ means understanding resistance. The table pairs protections with the movements that won them. Because they were won, they are reversible through **amendment, exemption and non-enforcement**, so watch for those routes.
notes.76: The Narmada movement lost the dam and changed the rules. Remember the table's last two rows: the dam was built, yet the World Bank withdrew after an independent review. The lasting result is that **displacement became a cost needing justification**, which reshaped how lenders assess resettlement worldwide.
notes.77: Niyamgiri is the clearest case of recognition justice operating through law. In 2013 the Supreme Court sent the decision on bauxite mining to the Gram Sabhas, and **every one consulted said no**. The precedent is cited widely and applied unevenly, so how a Gram Sabha is convened matters.
notes.78: In the POSCO case, villagers' resistance used the FRA and the Gram Sabha, and the company withdrew. The betel vine detail is the substance: the land counted as government land, so the compensation logic valued almost none of what was lost. **Land classification decided whether consent was required.**
notes.79: Fisherfolk lose spawning grounds, shore access and the catch to ports, thermal plants and reclamation. They are among the least visible groups because the resource is common, mobile and unmeasured: **there is no title to a fishery**. Track the Coastal Regulation Zone rules, which successive relaxations have narrowed.
notes.80: The slide groups resistance into five fronts: anti-nuclear, anti-mining, urban, coastal and riverine. They are separate movements with a shared structure: local, led by those affected and contesting a decision taken elsewhere. Networks give **legal capacity and visibility**, while the organising stays local.
notes.81: PIL lets any public-spirited person petition on behalf of others. Read the table as strengths and limits: broad standing against weak enforcement, direct relief against cost and delay. Treat a judgment as **a lever for what follows**. Use PIL when the political route is closed, and avoid filing first.
notes.82: Defending the environment can be dangerous, and the risk falls on local activists, especially Adivasi and rural ones, far more than on supporting organisations. The slide's advice is to **weigh the risk with the community** and say plainly that you can leave and they cannot.
notes.84: Polluter pays puts the cost of prevention and remedy on the cause. The right column is how it fails: insolvent polluters, disputed quantification, remediation not done and fines cheaper than compliance. In that last case the principle becomes **a licence fee**. Bhopal illustrates the second and third failures.
notes.85: Precaution says uncertainty is no reason to delay protection where harm may be serious or irreversible. The substance is the **shift in the burden of proof**: the proponent shows safety. The qualifiers 'serious' and 'irreversible' stop it becoming a veto, and that is where the argument happens.
notes.86: Under the public-trust doctrine the state is trustee of air, rivers, forests and seashores and has no right to treat them as owner. It entered Indian law through the Kamal Nath judgment (1996). Its force is that it **binds the government itself**, and it is better established than rights of nature on slide 90.
notes.87: Courts read a right to a healthy environment into Article 21, the right to life, with duties in Articles 48A and 51A(g). The slide's key point: **only Article 21 can be litigated directly**, and the other two give interpretive support. Outcomes can depend on which bench hears the matter.
notes.88: The NGT combines judicial and scientific members so technical evidence can be examined directly. It was established by statute in 2010 and can order relief and compensation. The practical limit is access: benches are few, and a distant community **needs legal support** to use it.
notes.89: The EIA is meant to deliver procedural justice and often falls short. The table lists the intended features against their weaknesses. Remember the structural problem: the proponent pays for the assessment. The hearing is still the formal moment to object, so **attend and get your objection minuted**.
notes.90: Rights of nature treats rivers and forests as rights-bearing entities. The table compares Ecuador, New Zealand and India, where the Uttarakhand ruling on the Ganga and Yamuna was stayed. The practical objection was liability. Public trust is the better-established cousin, **already applied in Indian judgments**.
notes.91: The toolkit has five tools: FRA and PESA, RTI, EIA hearings, the NGT and Article 21 PIL. Sequence them as the slide advises: **documents first, objection on record second, tribunal third, constitutional litigation last**. RTI is the cheapest and most under-used, so start there.
notes.93: Community monitoring turns 'we feel sick' into evidence. Low-cost monitors give data where official stations are absent, and a time series gives trend. Its value is as much political as technical. Anticipate the accuracy challenge by **pairing sensors with a protocol** and being honest about their limits.
notes.94: Mapping injustice is a method: sites against settlement, caste and income overlays, then health data. The slide says disaggregation is the whole method: **what you do not disaggregate, you cannot see**. Share the findings back with the community in their language.
notes.95: These five stance rules turn the framework into practice. The first changes your own work: ask who bears the harm of your project. The fourth is the cheapest: **disaggregate every figure** by caste, tribe, gender and distance, since most programme data already holds the categories you need.
notes.96: The traps are 'wasteland' that is really commons, token hearings, cash that erases an uncounted way of life, and unexamined green projects. The aim is **free, prior and informed consent**, which the slide describes as a sequence: before the decision, with full information and a real option to refuse.
notes.97: This slide is a source list: pollution boards for monitoring, emissions databases, the EJAtlas, FRA data, NGT judgments, and land and EIA documents via RTI. The slide calls the FRA data the most under-used: claims filed against titles granted shows **where community forest rights are recognised**.
notes.98: A short reading list pairs the Indian case, the comparative framework and the global history with the primary texts. The advice is to **read the Acts themselves**, since practitioners routinely misstate FRA and PESA on Gram Sabha consent. The last row is your first exercise: board data for your own district.
notes.99: Use the five takeaways as a closing self-test. Can you explain each in a sentence and point to one case from the deck? The fifth, **there is no empty land**, is the one practitioners most easily forget when a site is called wasteland.
